newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 2.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LEGAL AND PERSONNEL EXECUTIVES TOP LEAGUE

According to research from consultants Arthur Andersen, legal and personnel executives were at the top of the list for salaries in Britain's major public companies. The study found a strong relationship between salary and company size, and little evidence of "fat cat" executives. The consultants said that heads of legal and human resources departments were at the top end of the salary scale while heads of audit and tax were at the bottom.
-- BIDDERS IN LINE TO MANAGE SOCIAL SECURITY BUILDINGS

Three companies, Mapeley Holdings, a consortium led by stockbrokers Goldman Sachs and one led by Nomura of Japan, were set to submit bids to the government to take on a 20-year contract to run Britain's 700 social security offices. The groups were invited to offer 250 million stg for the contract, but the winner will be chosen on the level of service it will provide. The Department of Social Security offices were being offered as part of the private finance initiative.
-- OIL PRICES HEAT UP AS COLD SNAP BITES

Europe's cold New Year has led to a surge in oil and fuel prices, sparked a buying spree in heating oil and helped to push overall commodities indexes higher on the last trading day of 1996. February crude oil prices jumped by 55 cents, traders pushed the price of heating oil for January delivery up 2.27 cents and January petroleum rose by 1.06 cents.
THE TIMES
-- COMPUTER ERRORS MAY COST HALIFAX MEMBERS THEIR BONUS

Due to serious errors in the computer files at the Halifax, savers face losing share bonuses worth 1,000 stg on average when the building society converts to a bank. The Halifax has admitted that many savers have been sent the wrong information. This came within hours of the expiry of the New Year deadline for members to top up their savings to qualify for a bonus. Errors included being told they were ineligible for free shares, when they actually did qualify.
-- TAX AND RATES 'LIKELY TO RISE' AFTER ELECTION

According to the latest economic analysis by the independent think-tank, Cambridge Econometrics, taxes and interest rates will have to rise in the early days of a new parliament, whichever party wins the election. Cambridge emphasised that the incoming Administration will take power at a more auspicious time than in either 1974 or 1979 and argued that there is little prospect of the type of speculative boom seen in the recent past and the pain of the associated fallout.
-- US RULING OFFERS HOPE FOR UK CLAIMS

A ruling in the U.S. Tax Court in Washington, concerning a Canadian life insurance company which successfully argued that the Inland Revenue Service had violated the U.S.-Canada income tax treaty when it used a complex formula to assess the company's tax instead of the business's actual income, could lead to billions of dollars in claims for overpaid tax from British banks and other companies which have branch operations in the U.S.
THE GUARDIAN
-- MILLIONS 'CAN'T MOVE HOME'

Labour has undermined claims by the Government and leading organisations that the housing market is showing signs of recovery by releasing official statistics showing the number of households suffering from the scourge of "insufficient equality" has remained the same over the past two years. Alan Milburn, shadow Treasury spokesman, said the problem was preventing millions of people from moving home.
-- CABLE FIRMS PONDER BSKYB PRICE FIGHT

Cable companies will decide, in the middle of this month, whether to take legal action to force BSkyB to lower the price of some of its channels. Although executives from cable companies have not ruled out the prospect of further negotiations with the satellite broadcaster they regarded this as unlikely to result in success now the Office of Fair Trading has failed to support their claims that BSkyB should reduce the price of some of its programming.
-- AUDITORS BACK EXECUTIVE TESTS

The Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales was set to tell the Hampel committee on corporate governance that corporate governance rules should be rewritten to force executives to pass a "fit and proper" test before they can become directors of public companies. The accountants will also recommend that Hampel should insist that all directors put themselves up for re-election at least every three years.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FEAR FOR JOBS AS PITMAN TALKS OF OUTSOURCING TO INDIA

Sir Brian Pitman, chief executive of Lloyds TSB, was set to spark fresh fears of a massive new wave of job losses in the New Year after warning that the industry still employed too many people and should consider "outsourcing" services to countries like India. He told a group of business leaders that companies could benefit from "much lower costs" by contracting out many of their activities.
-- GRID REJECTS WIDESPREAD BLACKOUT FEARS

The National Grid has dismissed fears, from heavy industry users of electricity and power station chiefs, that Britain could face widespread blackouts as the electricity transmission system nears breaking point. The fears have been fuelled by worries that gas-fired power stations with interruptable supply contracts could be taken off-line and also by the surge in demand during peak periods which has occurred this winter.
-- WATER INDUSTRY OPERATES IN 'TAX-FREE ZONE'

Labour have renewed its assault on the privatised water companies, claiming that the new figures released by Ofwat, the industry watchdog, revealed that they paid virtually no mainstream corporation tax on their core activities last year. Frank Dobson, the party's environmental spokesman, described the industry as a "tax-free zone", saying that the ten water companies had paid almost no tax despite making 11 billion stg in profits and paying out 3.5 billion stg in dividends to shareholders since privatisation.
